summary: Aurelia is an interactive and educational space mission design game which simulates the real-world teamwork and collaboration on space missions, players can build and manage their own exploration mission. Aurelia is fully customisable. Players explore a 3D solar system, select a destination, design a spacecraft, choose an orbit and launch vehicle and balance engineering requirements such as mass, power, communication and budget. During flight, unexpected events require decisions that affect the mission outcome. Players can work alone with AI crew support or collaborate in teams of up to four. The game combines space-science data with simplified educational models to make mission design approachable. An academy and post-mission debrief help players understand the reasoning behind their choices and learn from the results.
details:
AURELIA lets players experience the decisions involved in designing and operating a space mission. Players explore destinations in a 3D solar system, select a mission, assemble a spacecraft, and check requirements including mass, propulsion, power, communications and cost. During a simulated flight, players respond to timed events and see the consequences in a mission debrief. The game also offers research progression, difficulty levels, a sandbox, design sharing and comparison, and cooperative multiplayer for up to four players. An academy explains concepts such as orbits, the rocket equation etc. Live data provides Moon and Mars distances, asteroid close approaches and space-weather information. Measurements and research references inform educational content, while the flight simulation and some resource estimates are simplified game models rather than predictions. We built the project with TypeScript, HTML and CSS, using Three.js for 3D graphics, GSAP for animation, Vite for building, and Node.js and WebSocket for multiplayer. GitHub Pages hosts the game and Render hosts the server. Music and effects are synthesised in the browser, and crew voices use the device’s speech engine. The project makes engineering trade off. Players learn by building, making decisions, seeing consequences and trying again.
